title: Guide to Sourdough Starter Ratios Using a Wooden Spurtle
meta_description: Master your sourdough starter feeding ratios with our practical guide. Learn how a wooden spurtle makes mixing and jar scraping easier for every baker.
html:
Getting your sourdough starter to peak consistently is less about magic and more about math. If your starter is sluggish or overflowing from the jar, the culprit is usually your feeding ratio. Understanding how to balance your seed starter, flour, and water allows you to control the fermentation speed and the acidity of your bread.

The secret to a clean, efficient feeding process isn't just the ingredients—it's the tools. Using a Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set (2 PCS) makes the process seamless. The skinny spurtle is designed specifically to reach the bottom corners of a mason jar, ensuring no pockets of dry flour remain, while the Danish-style stick handles the heavier lifting during the actual dough mix.

Understanding Sourdough Starter Feeding Ratios

A feeding ratio is expressed as Starter : Flour : Water. For example, a 1:1:1 ratio means equal parts by weight of each ingredient. If you use 50g of starter, you add 50g of flour and 50g of water.

Most beginners start with 1:1:1, but as you get more comfortable, you'll find that adjusting these ratios helps you manage your schedule. A lower ratio (like 1:1:1) peaks quickly, which is great for a morning bake. A higher ratio (like 1:5:5) slows down the fermentation, allowing you to feed your starter at night and have it ready by the next morning without it collapsing.

Common Ratios and When to Use Them

Depending on where you keep your starter (countertop vs. fridge) and the ambient temperature of your kitchen, you'll want to pivot your approach. Here are the most common sourdough starter feeding ratios:

  • 1:1:1 (The Standard): Best for reviving a sluggish starter or when you need a fast peak (usually 4-6 hours).
  • 1:2:2 (The Maintenance): A great middle-ground for room temperature storage; it keeps the yeast fed longer than a 1:1:1.
  • 1:5:5 (The Slow Burn): Ideal for overnight feeds or very warm summer kitchens to prevent the starter from becoming too acidic.
  • 1:10:10 (The Long Haul): Used by advanced bakers to keep a starter stable for 24+ hours without refrigeration.

The Role of the Wooden Spurtle in Feeding

If you've ever used a large metal spoon to feed your starter, you know the frustration of the "flour clump." Flour often gets trapped against the glass walls or stuck in the bottom curve of the jar. This is where the skinny wooden spurtle spatula shines.

Because of its slim profile, the spurtle acts as both a stirrer and a scraper. When you apply your sourdough starter feeding ratios, you can use the spurtle to incorporate the water into the seed starter first, breaking up the clumps, and then fold in the flour. The non-scratch wooden surface is gentle on your glassware and doesn't react with the acidity of the starter, unlike some low-quality metals.

Managing Starter Acidity and Waste

One of the biggest complaints in sourdough baking is the amount of "discard." If you feed a 1:1:1 ratio every day, you end up with a mountain of waste. By increasing your ratio—for example, moving to a 1:4:4—you can maintain a much smaller amount of "seed" starter while still providing enough food for the colony to thrive.

To keep your jar clean while using these ratios, use the Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set (2 PCS) to scrape down the sides of the jar after every feed. This prevents dried starter from crusting onto the glass, which can otherwise become a breeding ground for unwanted mold or bacteria.

Mixing the Final Dough

Once your starter has peaked according to your chosen ratio, it's time to mix your dough. While the skinny spurtle is king for the jar, the Danish-style dough stick in the set is the heavy hitter for the mixing bowl.

The open-loop design of the dough whisk allows you to incorporate the starter and flour without overworking the dough. It cuts through the sticky mass, blending the ingredients efficiently and ensuring your starter is evenly distributed throughout the loaf. This prevents "starter pockets" and leads to a more consistent crumb structure.

FAQ

Why isn't my starter peaking after a 1:1:1 feed?

Check your temperature. If your kitchen is cold, the yeast works slower. Try moving your jar to a warmer spot, like the top of the refrigerator, or use slightly warm water (around 80°F) during your feed.

Can I use different flours with the same ratios?

Yes, but keep in mind that whole grain flours (like rye or whole wheat) absorb more water than all-purpose flour. If you switch to a 100% rye feed, you may need to slightly increase the water in your ratio to keep the consistency stirrable.

How often should I change my feeding ratios?

Change them based on your schedule and season. Use higher ratios (1:4:4 or 1:5:5) in the summer or when you want to feed less often, and stick to lower ratios (1:1:1) in the winter or when prepping for a bake.
